Subject: Technical deep-dive recap: latency & throughput SLOs / deployment topology

Sarah / Acme team ���—

Thanks for the time today. Below is a concise recap of what we covered, the pain points you confirmed, and our recommended next steps. I’ve attached an SLO matrix version (acme-slo-matrix-20270220.xlsx) and a reference network/topology diagram (acme-network-topology-20270220.png).

Pain points & goals (as confirmed)
- Tail latency variability during bursty peak windows causing degraded UX (current p95 ~420ms for 512-token responses on-prem test)
- Need <120ms p95 for single-turn queries at 512 tokens; <220ms p95 for 2048-token contexts for premium customers
- Peak throughput expectation: sustained 25–35 req/s across the cluster with spikes to ~120 req/s for short bursts (1–2 minutes)
- Cost constraints: want to minimize per-token unit cost while meeting SLOs; open to mixed-model strategy

Key technical constraints you provided
- Typical prompt lengths average 120–350 tokens; worst-case context 2048 tokens
- Long-tail of users issue 1–2 requests concurrently per session; 5–8 concurrent sessions during spikes
- On-prem latency between customer edge and Redwood VPC varies (20–50ms) — network egress needs to be accounted for

Recommendations (summary)
1) Model strategy
   - Primary: LLaMA-variant ~70B quantized to int8 (recommended for quality), served on dedicated GPU pool for premium traffic
   - Fallback: 13B int8 for non-critical tiers to reduce latency/cost during high load or if KV cache miss rates are high
   - Consider a two-tier routing policy: stable traffic → 70B; overflow/burst → 13B or offload to batched async workers

2) Latency & serving optimizations
   - Targeted tail SLOs: p50/p95/p99 baselines captured in attached SLO matrix. For 512 tokens aim for p95 <120ms (single-turn); for 2048 tokens p95 <220ms.
   - Use continuous batching with small max-batch windows (5–10ms) for non-critical flows; VIP flows should be routed to single-request lanes with smaller batch sizes to meet tail SLOs
   - Enable KV/prefix caching for common prefixes to cut average token generation time and reduce cost

3) Deployment topology
   - Dedicated Redwood Dedicated pool in us-west-2 with autoscale policies:
     - Baseline nodes sized for sustained 30 req/s (70B serving), burst pool capacity to add ~4 nodes in <90s for spikes
     - Warm instances using proactive cache warming during predictable spikes (cron-based warmers)
   - VPC peering + private link for secure connectivity; TLS + customer-managed KMS for keys
   - Network considerations: ensure <50ms added RTT between your edge and serving region; if not, evaluate regional edge deploys or dedicated private deployment closer to traffic

4) Cost / quantization trade-offs
   - Int8 quantization provides significant cost savings with small quality delta for many generation tasks; evaluate int8-llm and q4f16 for a primary experiment
   - We’ll produce a cost/time-to-serve estimate for 70B int8 vs 13B int8 given your traffic profile (see attached cost sketch)

Action items / next steps
- Acme: share representative 48h traffic dump + a set of 10 canonical prompts (we can run evals) — Sarah
- Redwood: produce pilot sizing + cost estimate, initial performance baseline (p50/p95/p99) for 70B int8 and 13B int8 using your sample prompts — Marissa / Dev (ETA: 3 business days)
- Schedule: pilot kickoff targeted for Mar 1; pilot duration 2 weeks (collect metrics + refine autoscale) — Lauren to confirm calendar

Notes from the meeting that matter
- We agreed to a canary routing policy: 5% traffic on 70B initially to verify regressions; automated rollback if quality metrics drop
- Observability hooks: we’ll instrument per-request traces and token-level cost breakout; Redwood can export logs to your SIEM for audit

Attachments: acme-slo-matrix-20270220.xlsx, acme-network-topology-20270220.png
